The first 72 h following aneurysm rupture play a key role in determining clinical and cognitive outcomes after subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). Yet, very little is known about the impact of so called “early brain injury” on patents with clinically good grade SAH (as defined as World Federation of Neurosurgeons Grade 1 and 2). 27 patients with good grade SAH underwent MRI scanning were prospectively recruited at three time-points after SAH: within the first 72 h (acute phase), at 5–10 days and at 3 months. Patients underwent additional, comprehensive cognitive assessment 3 months post-SAH. 27 paired healthy controls were also recruited for comparison. In the first 72 h post-SAH, patients had significantly higher global and regional brain volume than controls. This change was accompanied by restricted water diffusion in patients. Persisting abnormalities in the volume of the posterior cerebellum at 3 months post-SAH were present to those patients with worse cognitive outcome. When using this residual abnormal brain area as a region of interest in the acute-phase scans, we could predict with an accuracy of 84% (sensitivity 82%, specificity 86%) which patients would develop cognitive impairment 3 months later, despite initially appearing clinically indistinguishable from those making full recovery. In an exploratory sample of good clinical grade SAH patients compared to healthy controls, we identified a region of the posterior cerebellum for which acute changes on MRI were associated with cognitive impairment. Whilst further investigation will be required to confirm causality, use of this finding as a risk stratification biomarker is promising. Wellcome Trust 203139/Z/16/Z issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2021 Introduction Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is a devastating disease with high mortality and morbidity in those patients who survive hospital treatment. Despite accounting for only 5% of all strokes, the socioeconomic cost of SAH has remained disproportionately high with a loss of functional years equivalent to ischaemic stroke. This is because despite reductions in the incidence of SAH 1 , 2 and mortality 3 , the disease often affects young adults of working age and frequently results in poor neurocognitive outcome 4 . Following successful aneurysm treatment, the management of patients with SAH is conventionally focused on the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of secondary brain injury caused by delayed cerebral ischaemia 5 . However, there is increasing evidence that damage caused in the first 72 h post-rupture—so called “early brain injury”—may play a key role not only in the development of such delayed cerebral ischaemia, but also in determining overall neurocognitive outcomes 6 . Early cerebral ischemia and infarction is common in the acute period after SAH and is associated with worse neurological and physiological admission status, as well as poor neurocognitive outcomes 7 , 8 . Global cerebral oedema is also a significant feature of early brain injury and is an independent risk factor for mortality and poor outcome after SAH 9 , 10 . Advances in MRI physics and analysis now offer a number of objective, reliable and non-invasive tools such as apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to measure changes in cerebral structure at a tissue level. The ADC is a measure of the diffusivity of water molecules in tissue. In ischemic tissue e.g. following SAH, cytotoxic edema leads to a reduction in the ADC suggesting that the ADC may be a good parameter for identification/quantification of cerebral edema 11 – 13 . Some of the main advantages to using a voxel-by-voxel approach such as VBM are that firstly, it is not biased to one particular structure, and gives a comprehensive assessment of anatomical differences throughout the entire brain without a priori knowledge of which regions may be affected. Furthermore, it is a fully automated process, and therefore is fully reproducible intra- and inter-rater 14 , 15 . For this reason, it is highly suited to the investigation of early brain injury due to the unpredictable nature of the physiological insult that occurs following aneurysm rupture. Furthermore, as early brain injury is characterised by cerebral oedema, using imaging techniques such as ADC and VBM that are sensitive to regional changes in brain tissue is particularly of value. The primary aim of this study was therefore to characterise imaging biomarkers of early brain injury in patients with good clinical grade SAH (WFNS 1 and 2). We aimed to quantify global and regional grey matter volume and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) in patients at three time points: within the first 72 h post-rupture, at 5–10 days and at 3 months post-SAH. We then investigated whether we could predict, within the acute period of the first 72 h post-SAH, the future incidence of cognitive impairment at 3 months post-SAH. Finally, we conducted an exploratory analysis relating our imaging findings with those from the UK Biobank to investigate possible genetic mechanisms underpinning any anatomical differences observed in those with poor cognitive outcome. Our study aimed to build a greater understanding of the pathophysiological changes incurred by aneurysm rupture, and to identify which patients—amongst those initially faring better—were most at risk of poor cognitive outcomes.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated imaging and cognitive biomarkers of early brain injury in good clinical grade aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) patients, and explored their ability to predict long-term cognitive impairment. It quantified global and regional brain volume, white matter volume, CSF volume, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values at acute (<72h), subacute (5-10 days), and chronic (3 months) phases post-SAH. Key findings include significantly higher global and regional brain volume and restricted water diffusion (lower ADC) acutely, persistent abnormalities in posterior cerebellar volume at 3 months correlating with worse cognitive outcomes, and the ability of acute cerebellar gray matter changes to predict cognitive impairment at 3 months with 84% accuracy. The study also explored genetic associations with cerebellar gray matter volume, linking several genetic variants to cardiovascular disease and other health indicators.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of early brain injury and cognitive impairment following aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) using MRI and cognitive assessments.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 27 good-grade SAH patients (WFNS 1 and 2) underwent MRI scanning and comprehensive cognitive assessment at three time-points: within the first 72 hours (acute phase), at 5-10 days (subacute phase), and at 3 months (chronic phase) post-SAH. An additional 27 paired healthy controls were recruited for comparison. No specific therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were investigated, as this was an observational study of SAH's natural course and sequelae.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in patients compared to healthy controls within 72 hours post-SAH; trends towards higher at 5-10 days; no significant difference at 3 months.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Overall structural size of the brain, sensitive to cerebral oedema/swelling.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute (< 72 hours), subacute (5-10 days), and chronic (3 months) phases post-SAH.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute brain swelling or edema early after SAH, which resolves by 3 months post-SAH.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Brain (measured via MRI using SIENA-X & Voxel-based Morphometry - VBM)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher (median 80% higher) in patients compared to healthy controls within 72 hours post-SAH, with widespread regional increases (anterior cingulate/paracingulate gyrus, primary motor cortex, left supramarginal and angular gyrus, fusiform gyrus (right), basal ganglia, cerebellum). Trends towards higher at 5-10 days (less marked but prominent in cerebellum); no significant difference in whole-brain average at 3 months.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute widespread GM swelling or edema early after SAH, which largely resolves globally by 3 months, though regional differences persist.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the diffusivity of water molecules in tissue; a decrease indicates restricted diffusion due to cellular swelling (cytotoxic oedema).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute (< 72 hours), subacute (5-10 days), and chronic (3 months) phases post-SAH.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Highly indicative of cytotoxic cerebral oedema early after SAH; suggests continued or resolving changes in GM microstructure in the subacute phase, with resolution of global abnormalities by 3 months.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Regional Cerebellar Gray Matter (GM) Volume (Lobule VII & VIIIa)
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Cerebellum (measured via MRI VBM, specifically lobule VII: Crus II, Crus I, VIIb and VIIIa)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Patients who later developed cognitive impairment at 3 months post-SAH already showed a significant apparent higher GM volume in an overlapping cerebellar region (extending into lobules VIIb and VIIIa) at scan 1 (acute phase). This acute measure discriminated patients with vs. without cognitive impairment with 84% accuracy (sensitivity 82%, specificity 86%, AUC 0.805). Persistent and significantly higher GM volume in patients compared to controls (mainly lobule VII: Crus II, Crus I, and VIIb) was observed at 3 months, with cognitively impaired patients having higher GM volumes (Cohen's d = 0.72).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Volume of gray matter in cerebellar regions associated with motor control, coordination, and higher cognitive functions; indicator of cellular swelling/cytotoxic oedema.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute (< 72 hours) and chronic (3 months) phases post-SAH; predictive of future cognitive outcomes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A promising risk stratification biomarker for predicting future cognitive impairment at 3 months post-SAH, even in patients initially appearing clinically good grade. Persistent abnormalities are linked to worse cognitive outcomes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 11 out of 25 patients diagnosed with cognitive impairment based on lower N-ISAT scores.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Assessment of global cognitive function, with specific impairment in executive skills, processing speed, and non-verbal skills.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cognitively impaired patients had significantly lower ACE-R scores (89 \u00b1 5) compared to non-impaired patients (93 \u00b1 5, p = 0.03 Mann\u2013Whitney test).

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cognitive testing at 3 months post-SAH in patients diagnosed with cognitive impairment.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences between cognitively impaired and non-impaired patients.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Genetic association with cerebellar GM volume (Crus I)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant association with cerebellar GM volume (Crus I). The most strongly associated locus (rs72754248, p = 1.4 \u00d7 10\u221217) correlated significantly with two primary causes of death: Emphysema (ICD10 J43.9, p = 2 \u00d7 10\u22125) and Accidental exposure to other and unspecified factors (ICD10 X59.5, p = 3.6 \u00d7 10\u22126). Serum PAPP-A concentration also emerges as a predictor of risk for poor outcome in transient ischemic attack and ischemic stroke.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Predictor of poor outcome in ischemic events and associated with heightened risk for specific causes of death.
